+---
+"Basic mlt query with docs - explicitly on same shard":
+  - skip:
+      version: "all"
+      reason: temporarily disabling for investigation
+
+  - do:
+      indices.create:
+        index: mlt_one_shard_test_index
+        body:
+          settings:
+            index:
+              number_of_shards: 1
+              number_of_replicas: 0
+
+  - do:
+      index:
+        index:  mlt_one_shard_test_index
+        id:     "1"
+        body:   { foo: bar }
+
+  - do:
+      index:
+        index:  mlt_one_shard_test_index
+        id:     "2"
+        body:   { foo: baz }
+
+  - do:
+      index:
+        index:  mlt_one_shard_test_index
+        id:     "3"
+        body:   { foo: foo }
+
+  - do:
+      indices.refresh: {}
+
+  - do:
+      get:
+        index: mlt_one_shard_test_index
+        id: "1"
+
+  - match: { _source.foo: "bar" }
+
+  - do:
+      get:
+        index: mlt_one_shard_test_index
+        id: "2"
+
+  - match: { _source.foo: "baz" }
+
+  - do:
+      get:
+        index: mlt_one_shard_test_index
+        id: "3"
+
+  - match: { _source.foo: "foo" }
+
+  - do:
+      search:
+        rest_total_hits_as_int: true
+        index:   mlt_one_shard_test_index
+        body:
+          query:
+            more_like_this:
+              like:
+                -
+                  _index: mlt_one_shard_test_index
+                  doc:
+                    foo: bar
+                -
+                  _index: mlt_one_shard_test_index
+                  _id: "2"
+                -
+                  _id: "3"
+              include: true
+              min_doc_freq: 0
+              min_term_freq: 0
+
+  - match: { hits.total: 3 }

+# Explanation of files in this directory
+
+`rsa-private-jwkset.json`, `rsa-public-jwkset.json`
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+These files are created by running the tests in `JwtRealmGenerateTests`.
+
+Those tests generate the yaml settings, the keystore settings and the JWK Sets
+for each sample realm.
+
+Copy the output from the test output into the applicable file (you may wish to
+run it through `jq` first in order to make it more readable).
+
+-------
+
+If additional keys are needed (e.g. to add more algorithms / key sizes) we can
+either extend the existing JWKSets with another set of keys (that is, modify the
+existing method in `JwtRealmGenerateTests` so that it creates more keys in the
+same JWKSet, then re-run and replace the files on disk) or create new files (
+that is, add another test to `JwtRealmGenerateTests` that creates the relevant
+realm and/or JWKSet, then re-run and add the new files to disk).

timeline.body:
Fixes https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/101763
Fixes https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/102393. Tests updates pending.

This change will make queries that don't need any fields from the `_field_caps` call to actually ask only for `_index` field, instead of asking all of them. This will make the `_field_caps` call itself much lighter and its response size almost inexistent (it contains only the list of indices and `_index`).

This is the meat of the PR. All the scenarios tested proved that asking here for `_index` instead of `*` is enough. `fieldNames` method identifies well (so far) all the situations where `*` is needed.

This trick here makes the whole analysis of FieldCapabilitiesResponse to accept metadata fields (even if by design the [IndexResolver skips them](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/102510/files#diff-341e59a86f203e72508f62dcce2aa897af639103da85ea5671d557f33109c1a9L710)) but only to allow the list of indices to be built. This is important for [this kind of issue](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/102393) where an empty list of indices in this method's result [will not make the compute service happy](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/plugin/ComputeService.java#L141).

timeline.body: Hi @astefan, I've updated the changelog YAML for you.

nit: I feel like empty normally means "no rows" rather than "no fields". Maybe this should be called `NoFieldsRelation` or `EmptyMappingRelation` so to make that clear. Maybe a small javadoc would also be nice, explaining that this is specifically intended for ~indexes with empty mapping~ when we request 0 fields from an index.
super nit/question: why is this needed? A small comment would help (me) understand this list's purpose :)

reply.body: If this list is empty we optimize/prune away empty plans. An empty plan is defined by having an empty list of attributes as its `output()`.

Yeah, I think that would be great as a small comment as this is not obvious.

The optimization rules could also probably look for `EmptyEsRelation` specifically and not prune that; or we may not prune if there's an indication that we need a metadata field, even if there's no non-meta attributes. But IMHO a comment would be sufficient + helpful.

Thanks for clarifying in any case!

I think there is a balance as to how much commented code there is and how much unwritten knowledge there is. Some things are not obvious and where my gut feeling tells me some comments are needed, I add them in code or I put something in the PR itself.

There are also places where things can be explained in reviews like these ^ without filling the Java code with comments. Pruning empty plans is knowledge related to the Optimizer and who is reviewing such a PR has a basic knowledge of the Optimizer and I believe it's enough to either answer a question here or offline if needed.

Generally I agree; I think, however, that the Optimizer is quite unrelated code to this, so needing to think about implementation details in the Optimizer may add a bit of confusion if someone else picks up work on this some months later.

But yeah, it's minor so this is fine :)

timeline.body: super nit: if possible, I think it'd be a tad cleaner to return an empty set here and then check for emptiness when calling `fieldnames`; mapping "no field names found" to "let's just use `_index`" sounds like the (pre-) analyzer's job, and I'd rather expect `fieldnames` to just return what fieldnames it finds in the plan.

reply.body:
So, there are three situations here:
- just a regular list of fields extracted from the plan. Like `from test | keep first_name`
- all fields, simply because they are needed: `from test`
- and no fields at all because we don't need to read anything from Lucene `from test | stats count(*)`
`fieldNames()` job is to decide what `_field_caps` will use in its call.
On one hand  having all this logic in this static method helps greatly with unit testing.
On the other hand, there is logic outside `fieldNames` that changes its content already, like fields needed for enrich policies.

I'll have another look at this. For unit testing's sake, I think I will integrate the enrich policies default match fields logic inside `fieldNames` and add some more tests to `IndexResolverFieldNamesTests`.
To clarify, this minor remark is meant as highly optional. Nice-to-have if `fieldnames`'s responsibility vs. `preAnalyzeIndices` would be super clear, but not worth putting in real effort IMO :)

I've reworked this. Mostly because of how enrich policies were handled, and it turned out there was a small improvement there. Thanks for raising the discussion point. Even though I haven't addressed your exact concern, something was definitely improved there.

reply.body: Imo, the logic is too simple to warrant a separate method. Not-null set and a `contains`....

But then why extract it as variable? :) It'd be small and inlined, code dedup'ing and easier to read (especially in the loop above).

timeline.body:
nit: I guess this has to be in sync with what we do in `preAnalyzeIndices`. Is there maybe a way to refactor this and/or `preAnalyzeIndices` to enforce this (maybe by calling into the same helper function or so)? Specifically, it may be important that we use the same validity verifier, field updater and allowed metadata as in `EsqlSession`.

Otherwise, future changes to `preAnalyzeIndices` might accidentally not lead to test failures here.

reply.body:
There's no easy way to do this kind of testing and, also, keeping it light.
The logic in `preAnalyzeIndices` calls in logic from `IndexResolver` which, in turn is creating a `field_caps` request (and possibly other requests related to aliases and CCS) that goes to ES. The call here is a simplified one where the field_caps response is emulated. What if the field_caps response format changes? This test will not protect us from this.

There is a balance here: test very thoroughly and create IT tests that use the exact code from `preAnalyzeIndices` or isolate the needed logic and do unit tests. I looked into IT tests because of the field_caps output I needed, but I decided it's too much and used unit tests instead. Also, there is another problem with the IT tests: they do not actually look at how the field_caps response look like and how the Analyzer is behaving in that case; the only thing you could assert on is the outcome of a query. OR create more elaborate mocking tests that allows you to run a `field_caps` call as close to reality as possible and then stop the ESQL logic at the analyzer level and look how the analysis is performed. Imo, it's too much work and resources for not so much gain.
